text: Three married men bury a friend their own age, and then decline to go home. What follows has 131 minutes and almost no plot to spend them on: drinking, talk that overshoots its point, a decision to leave the country taken with about as much deliberation as ordering another round. Cassavetes lets scenes run well past the moment they have made their point, and the discomfort that produces is the actual subject. Leaving the country is presented not as a decision but as the same evening continuing by other means. These three are funny. They are also working hard at being funny, in front of each other, because the alternative is to say plainly what the funeral told them. Wives and children stay offstage and never once leave the room.

The crime at the centre of it sounds like a prank, and the film treats it with total seriousness for 125 minutes. Britain, 1944: three travellers stop short of Canterbury in a small town and set about finding out who is responsible. What they mostly turn up is the town itself, its roads, its work, its long habit of being walked through by pilgrims on their way somewhere holier. Powell and Pressburger were making this while the war was still being fought, and the choice shows in what the film slows down for: fields, weather, an afternoon no investigation requires. The mystery is real and it is also a pretext, a reason to hold three people in one place long enough for the place to work on them. Canterbury waits at the end of the road the whole time. Nobody hurries.

A submarine picture has nowhere to put its people: one steel tube, the same faces, for as long as the story runs. Petersen takes 150 minutes and treats that as the premise rather than the problem. The boat hunts, then finds itself hunted, and the crew's work becomes waiting, reading a gauge, listening to the hull, doing arithmetic on the air. It is a German film about the German war effort, and it puts the audience below the waterline with the crew rather than above it. Made in 1981, it refuses to settle what these men were: conscripted labour inside a machine built to kill, frightened in a way that has nothing to do with whether they deserve to be. What holds it is duration. The loudest events are a sound in the water and a number on a dial, and both are allowed to sit there until they stop being abstract.

A six-year-old is told to bury the totems of his childhood in the sand, and does. From there the desert is the only set there is: a gunfighter riding out to face the masters one after another, in a structure lifted whole from the western and then put to purposes the western never had. Jodorowsky shot it in Mexico in 1969 and made no attempt to hide the parable. The duels are lessons, the wounds are arguments, and the film would rather be read as ritual than followed as plot. It holds a place on Somos: 100 mejores del cine mexicano, an accounting made at home rather than abroad. It is violent without being kinetic, slow without being still. The images arrive with a flat confidence that refuses to apologise for itself, and 125 minutes of open desert leaves nowhere else to look.

Clay first, and everything after that is consequence: the creature carries the weight of the material it was dug out of, and the film keeps returning to that weight. Sixteenth-century Prague, persecution bearing down on the Jewish quarter, a rabbi who answers it by shaping a servant out of the ground and waking it with sorcery. Eighty-five silent minutes, made in Germany in 1920, from a legend belonging to a city and to a people under threat inside it. What the rabbi undertakes is a bargain rather than a rescue: protection bought by making something stronger than the people it protects, and then keeping that thing obedient, with nothing to guarantee the second part. Boese builds the whole picture on that single unstable clause. The horror is not the monster. It is the terms.

A wall goes up at the edge of a village: no door, no window, and a man on the other side of it. The woman he was travelling with finds a way through, and the figure waiting there is Death, whom the German title calls weary, which is the measure of the adversary. He answers her with three stories set far from the inn where the evening began, each arranged so that a woman must try to keep a man alive. Lang's interest is in the frame more than the tales, in the same appeal made three times to someone who has heard it before, in a film where the distant settings are frankly sets and only the bargaining is treated as real. Ninety-eight minutes, 1921, and the spectacle keeps giving way to something closer to a procedure.

A man sells fruit from a barrow, and his family cannot forgive him for it. Everything in Fassbinder's 88 minutes runs off that single fact: the drinking, the violence at home, the heart that gives out under a weight nobody in the room will name. Hans is neither stupid nor blameless, which is the difficulty. His relatives get to be right about him in small ways while being monstrous in the large one, and the film relieves neither side of that. It stays domestic in the strictest sense, all interiors, a marriage, people who have known each other far too long to bother being careful. West Germany, 1972. What is unusual is the scale: a trade, a wife, a relative's opinion, chosen because that is the scale at which this kind of damage actually gets done.

Her father owns the pharmacy; the man who assaults her works behind its counter. What the household does next is the film's real business, not the crime but the arrangement that follows it, in which a pregnant daughter becomes a question of reputation and is removed from the house on those grounds. Pabst made it in Germany in 1929, at the end of the silent period, so the entire argument is carried in faces and in what people do with their hands. Thymian is not written to be pitied. She is written as someone paying close attention, and 113 minutes is long enough to see what fending for herself teaches her and what it costs. The cruelty is procedural, conducted by respectable people following rules they did not have to invent. Not one of them would call the day's business cruelty.

One turkey, and a starving man who intends to eat all of it himself. Macario carries that wish through a Day of the Dead, and when three visitors ask him to share, his answers become the plot: he feeds only Death, and is paid in a bottle of water that cures any illness. From there the film moves at the speed of a folk tale. The healings, the money, the village doctor overtaken, the Inquisition beginning to wonder where a peasant came by such a gift. Roberto Gavaldón takes 91 minutes and never breaks the fable's logic to explain itself. Mexico sent it to the Academy Awards as its entry. Hunger is the first fact of the story and it never entirely leaves. What unsettles is not the bargain but how quickly an ordinary hungry man learns to price the thing he now controls.

The revenge is clerical: one word typed onto another person's blood test. Tomás Tomás keeps a diary full of women and no intention of being reached by any of them, and when one of them writes positive where negative belonged, he sets about arranging his own death with the same efficiency he had brought to avoiding everyone. Cuarón shot it in Mexico City in 1991, and the year is what gives the joke its edge, because the word on that page carried then exactly what it carried. A misprint is a thin thing on which to hang ninety minutes, and the film knows it and presses down anyway: timing, doors, near misses, farce at speed. Under the speed is something colder, a man who built a life nobody could enter and is now discovering that it holds.

Germany, 1940: the subject is Süß Oppenheimer, treasurer to Duke Karl Alexander of Württemberg, and the film assembled around him is a Nazi historical drama in the plain sense of those words. Nothing in it is accidental. That is why it is still catalogued among the consequential German films, not as drama, but as evidence of what a fully equipped national cinema can be aimed at when the state does the aiming. Veit Harlan had costume, score, crowd scenes and a competent narrative line, and every one of those instruments is at work here on one purpose. Ninety-five minutes, and each of them was built to do something to the person watching. The craft is ordinary. The purpose is not. The distance between the two is the whole of the case.

Two enterprises operate in the same London: one runs the thieves, the other licenses the beggars, and a marriage has just joined them without the second one's consent. Pabst filmed it in Germany in 1931, a turn-of-the-century London assembled from a distance, where theft is a trade and charity runs a payroll. Mack the Knife has the charm of a well-run business. Peachum, father of the bride, is the more frightening man, because his product is pity and he can put it on the street at scale. Nothing here is really about vice; it is about territory, tariffs, and who is licensed to collect. The songs are not relief. They are commentary, sung by people who go straight back to work when the number ends. A hundred and twelve minutes of hard, clean bookkeeping about who eats.

The title names 1918; the film was made in 1930, close enough that much of its first audience had been in those trenches. Four German infantrymen hold a stretch of line in France, and their time is organised not around battle but around alternation: the trench, then a village behind the lines and a few hours of not being shot at, then the trench again. Pabst spends 97 minutes letting that rhythm stand in for a whole life. The original title counts the men rather than the battles: four of the infantry. When Karl takes leave and goes home, the war he finds there is being fought over food and rent, and his family has been losing it. Nothing is arranged to be heroic and nobody makes a speech about waste. The camera holds still while the shelling starts again, which turns out to be the harder argument.

A rescue that ought to change everything changes nothing: he is still penniless and she is still a countess. Balduin pulls Margit out of the water in Prague, 1820, and the distance between what he has done and what he can have drives everything after. He has saved her life, which here earns him gratitude and nothing convertible. A German production of 1913 borrowed the city and the period for their old streets and their convenient remove, and at 85 minutes, when the feature was still an argument rather than a habit, that is a long stretch to give to one young man's wish. The fantasy enters exactly where the money should have been. Cinema this early is usually watched with allowances made for it; this one holds, because the wanting at its centre needs no translation into a modern idiom.
